summary.description: Two or three sentences on what this change does and where its risk sits. Goes at the top of the posted review.

notes.description: Anything about the run rather than the code: a lens that returned nothing, a skill that would not load, coverage you believe is missing. Reported to the author as caveats, so say what you could not check.

resolve.description: Threads to mark resolved. Judge each one; there is no mechanical rule behind this.

reason.description: One line on why this thread is finished, shown in the review so a wrong call is visible.

lens_health.description: One entry per lens you dispatched, including any that failed or returned nothing.

ok.description: False when the lens errored, could not load its skill, or returned an unusable response.

detail.description: What this lens could not check, in its own words, and why it returned what it did. The only per-lens line a reader sees, so a lens's coverage limits belong here whatever its finding count.

status.description: 'already-reported' when a comment on this pull request already describes the defect, whoever wrote it. 'declined' when a reply rejected it or chose not to act. Only 'new' findings get posted. When in doubt say 'new': a repeated comment is a small cost, a suppressed finding is one nobody sees.

existing_comment_url.description: The url of the thread that covers this finding, when a thread is what settled it. A finding matched against the previous run's findings has no comment of its own, so leave this out in that case.

found_by.description: Every lens that independently reported this defect. More than one entry means it was deduplicated, which is corroboration worth surfacing.

line.description: The single most specific line the finding is about.

end_line.description: Only for a genuine multi-line range.

in_diff.description: False when this line is not part of the reviewed diff. Report it either way: the review is a comment on the pull request rather than on a line, so nothing is dropped for sitting outside the diff.

body.description: The problem and the fix. When several lenses described it, keep what each added rather than flattening to the shortest version.

risk.description: How much this finding matters, as answers a diff can support rather than one overall word. Every axis is required; answer `not-applicable` where the question does not apply to this kind of defect rather than guessing, because a guess is scored and a stated non-answer is not. review/risk.ts turns these into a number and a tier; nothing here is a tier.

impact.description: The worst outcome that could realistically follow if this defect is left in. catastrophic: Arbitrary code execution, total data loss, or funds moved wrongly. serious: Data disclosed or corrupted, authentication bypassed, or a feature broken for everyone. moderate: A feature works incorrectly in a way a user would notice and report. minor: Cosmetic, or wrong only in an edge case nobody depends on. none: Nothing goes wrong. A style or clarity point.

data_exposure.description: What data this puts at risk, and whether losing it would be reportable. regulated: Health, payment card, or personal data whose breach is reportable under GDPR, PCI DSS or HIPAA. credentials: Tokens, keys, passwords or session material. personal: Data identifying a person, without a specific reporting duty attached. internal: Business data that is not public and not about a person. none: No data is exposed.

blast_radius.description: How much is affected when this goes wrong, rather than how badly. system: The whole deployment, or data belonging to every tenant. all-users: Every user of one tenant or one installation. tenant: One organisation's data, where others are unaffected. single-user: Only the person who triggers it, their own data included. none: Nothing is affected at run time.

reversibility.description: Whether the damage can be undone once it has happened. irreversible: Deleted data with no backup, a leaked secret, or a settled payment. costly: Recoverable, but only by hand, from backups, or with a migration. reversible: Undone by fixing the code and re-running. not-applicable: Nothing happens that would need undoing.

detectability.description: Whether anyone would find out this had happened. silent: No error, no log, no alert. Wrong numbers or missing records that look correct. delayed: Discovered eventually, by reconciliation, a report, or a user complaint. obvious: Fails loudly: an exception, a failed request, a broken page. not-applicable: Nothing happens at run time to detect.

availability.description: What this costs in liveness or resources. outage: Can take the service down: unbounded query, exhaustion, deadlock, no timeout. degradation: Measurably slower or heavier under ordinary load. none: No effect on liveness. not-applicable: Not code that runs under load.

contract.description: Whether this breaks a rule that is written down somewhere, rather than one you are applying. standard: Violates a named external standard: a WCAG criterion, an RFC, a documented API contract. house-rule: Violates this repository's own written conventions, REVIEW.md included. none: No written rule covers it. The claim rests on your judgement.

maintenance.description: What this costs to live with, if nothing ever goes wrong at run time. This is the axis for a defect that is expensive rather than dangerous. compounding: Gets worse on its own: a rule with no check behind it, an invariant stated in prose that the next edit will break silently. duplicated: The same fact or logic in more than one place, with nothing keeping the copies in step. untested: Logic with no test, where a wrong change would pass every gate. friction: Costs a reader or an editor time: misleading naming, a stale comment, a hard-to-follow structure. none: No ongoing cost. Fixing it is the whole of the work. not-applicable: A hazard rather than a cost, so what it would cost to live with is not the question.

likelihood.description: How likely the bad outcome is to be reached in practice, not how bad it would be. certain: Happens every time the code runs. likely: Happens under ordinary use, without anyone trying. possible: Needs an unusual input, a specific sequence, or deliberate effort. unlikely: Needs a race, a rare configuration, or several things to go wrong at once. theoretical: No path you can actually construct, though the shape is wrong. not-applicable: Nothing goes wrong at run time, so there is no outcome to be likely. A maintenance cost rather than a hazard.

confidence.description: How sure you are the defect is real, having read the code rather than recognised a pattern. confirmed: Traced in the code. You can name the path from input to damage. probable: Strongly implied by what you read, without following every branch. possible: Consistent with the code, but it depends on something you could not see. speculative: A recognised shape. You have not confirmed it does what you suspect.

privileges_required.description: What someone must already have in order to trigger this. none: Anonymous. No account, no session. user: Any ordinary authenticated account. elevated: An administrator, or a role granted deliberately. maintainer: Someone who can already deploy or push code, so could do the damage anyway. not-applicable: Not something anyone triggers.

attack_vector.description: Where this can be reached from. network: Over the internet, by anyone who can reach the service. local: Only from the machine, or from inside the network boundary. ci: Only through the build or deployment pipeline. push-access: Only by someone who can already commit to this repository. not-applicable: Not reachable by anybody. A correctness or clarity defect.

timing.description: Whether this is exploitable now or only under conditions that do not hold yet. live: Exploitable against the code as it stands. latent: Needs a future caller, a config change, or more data than exists today. not-applicable: Not a question of timing.
